title: Convergence of Regret Matching in Potential Games and Constrained Optimization
claim: One algorithm variant reliably converges to a stationary point within a few iterations, while the baseline stays stuck at high error.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared y-axis, very different x-axis scales
description: Two side-by-side matplotlib line plots share a y-axis labeled KKT gap, running from 0 to 1, with dashed grid lines and a blue curve in each. The left panel, titled Regret matching, has an x-axis of iteration count up to 100000. Its curve stays flat at 1.0 and shows only a few brief downward spikes, at about 0, 1000, 8000 and 61000 iterations. The right panel, titled Regret matching+, has an x-axis that runs only to 250 iterations. Its curve oscillates and falls for the first roughly 45 iterations, then drops to exactly 0 and stays there. The two x-axis scales differ by orders of magnitude, which is what the eye notices first. The contrast between the stuck curve and the converging curve makes the point.
caption: Illustration of our main results: $\RMplus$ always converges fast to a KKT point while $\RM$ can take exponential time even in two-player identical-interest games, constructed in [ref].
abstract: Regret matching (RM) -- and its modern variants -- is a foundational online algorithm that has been at the heart of many AI breakthrough results in solving benchmark zero-sum games, such as poker. Yet, surprisingly little is known so far in theory about its convergence beyond two-player zero-sum games. For example, whether regret matching converges to Nash equilibria in potential games has been an open problem for two decades. Even beyond games, one could try to use RM variants for general constrained optimization problems. Recent empirical evidence suggests that they -- particularly regret matching$^+$ (RM$^+$) -- attain strong performance on benchmark constrained optimization problems, outperforming traditional gradient descent-type algorithms. We show that RM$^+$ converges to an $Îµ$-KKT point after $O_Îµ(1/Îµ^4)$ iterations, establishing for the first time that it is a sound and fast first-order optimizer. Our argument relates the KKT gap to the accumulated regret, two quantities that are entirely disparate in general but interact in an intriguing way in our setting, so much so that when regrets are bounded, our complexity bound improves all the way to $O_Îµ(1/Îµ^2)$. From a technical standpoint, while RM$^+$ does not have the usual one-step improvement property in general, we show that it does in a certain region that the algorithm will quickly reach and remain in thereafter. In sharp contrast, our second main result establishes a lower bound: RM, with or without alternation, can take an exponential number of iterations to reach a crude approximate solution even in two-player potential games. This represents the first worst-case separation between RM and RM$^+$. Our lower bound shows that convergence to coarse correlated equilibria in potential games is exponentially faster than convergence to Nash equilibria.
